title: How to handle candidate counteroffer negotiation on Mac: steps for recruiters in 2026
metaTitle: Handle candidate counteroffer negotiation: recruiter steps for Mac
description: Handle candidate counteroffer negotiation before the pushback starts. Costs, causes, free fixes, and a week plan for recruiters on a Mac.
intro: To handle candidate counteroffer negotiation, find out the real number and the real reason before the offer call. Pushback is easier to plan for than to fix in the last hour. This guide covers what counteroffers cost, why they happen, fixes you can use without buying anything, and where Lazur helps on a Mac.
tldr: Ask what would make the candidate say yes before you name a new number.
In a Gallup survey, 45% of people who voluntarily left said no leader talked with them about their future in the three months before they left.
Pew found only 28% of workers who asked for more pay than their first offer got the pay they asked for.
Counteroffer retention figures conflict, so treat any single number as a rough signal.
Put the gap in a sheet, pre-approve a range, and reply in writing the same day.

blocks.text: A candidate counteroffer usually comes one of two ways. The candidate asks you for more after you extend an offer. Or their current employer makes them a counter to stay. Both can land at a bad time, close to a start date. You cannot control the other employer. You can control what you know before the call, and how fast you reply.
Why counteroffers catch recruiters off guard

Many recruiters hear the pushback after the offer is already out. The number is in writing, so changing it feels like a loss. Some candidates raise money late, if they raise it at all. Pew Research reported in 2023 that most U.S. workers did not ask for higher pay when they were hired. Among workers who asked for more than their first offer, 28% got the pay they asked for. Another 38% got more than the original offer, but less than they asked. The other 35% got only the original offer. That survey covered starting-salary talks, not counteroffers. The sample was not a random sample of job seekers, so read the split as a pattern, not a rate.
What a counteroffer costs your team

The salary gap is only part of the bill. Gallup estimates replacing a worker costs about 200% of salary for leaders and managers. It estimates 80% for technical professionals and 40% for frontline employees. Those are estimates, not a measurement of your company. Still, they show why a careful week of talks can beat a quick no. A failed counteroffer also means a second search, more interviews, and a hiring manager who waits longer.
Which counteroffer retention numbers to trust

Counteroffer retention figures disagree, and many circulate without a source. Some of the numbers are secondhand. You will also see a very high leave-within-a-year figure online. Do not use it. We found no study that traced it to a primary source. The table sorts the figures you can cite from the ones you should not.

blocks.caption: Counteroffer figures and how much weight each one can carry
rows: 65% of employees who accepted a counteroffer stayed at least two more years. Sample: 212 hiring managers.
Small and employer-reported. Use it as a signal.

50% of employees who accept a counteroffer leave within 12 months.
Secondhand. The original CEB report was not read.
HBR podcast page, citing Heidrick & Struggles

Shows candidate fear, not what actually happens.

blocks.text: Read the first two rows together. One says most people stay. The other says half leave within a year. That gap is the point. A counteroffer can hold someone for a while. It often does not fix what made them look. SHRM put it this way: if the offer doesn't address what's driving an employee to leave, it isn't likely to keep that employee onboard for good.
How to prepare before the offer call

Prep is where most of the value sits. Spend a short block of time before the call on three questions. What is the real number they need? What else do they want? Who can approve a change, and how fast?

items: Write the offer you can make, and the highest you can approve, in one row of a sheet.
Ask the candidate what would make them say yes, before you name a new number.
Find out whether a competing offer exists and when it expires.
Confirm who signs off on a pay change, and how long that usually takes.
Note non-pay items you can offer, such as a review date, a title, or a start date.

blocks.text: Here is a worked example with no real names. Put your offer in column B and the candidate's ask in column C. Then type =C2-B2 in cell D2 and copy it down. Column D shows the gap. If the gap is bigger than your approval, you know before the call. You need a different lever, or the answer is no.
Handling the pushback call, step by step

Call first, then send the email. A call lets you hear tone. An email locks the terms. Open by thanking the candidate for being direct. Then ask one open question. What would make you feel good about signing this week?

items: Let them finish. Write the ask down as they say it.
Restate the ask in one sentence, so you know you heard it right.
Ask what is driving the change: pay, title, scope, location, or timing.
Say what you can approve today, and what needs a check with the hiring manager.
Agree on a time for a written reply, then keep that time.

blocks.text: Do not promise a number you have not approved. Do not say you will match a competing offer unless policy allows it. If they name another employer, ask for the key terms, and say you will confirm what you can do. A calm, specific reply beats a fast, vague yes.
Writing the reply in Gmail

Put the agreed terms in writing the same day. Open the thread in Gmail and click Reply. To send later, click the arrow next to Send > Schedule send. Scheduled sends help when the candidate is in another time zone. They also keep a late-night email from reading like a rush.

Keep the email short. State the base pay, the start date, and the review date. Name the one item that changed. Ask for a written reply by a set date. Leave out a candidate's pay history. Leave out a competing employer's name unless you must include it. Your company may have rules on candidate personal data.
Mistakes recruiters make with counteroffers

items: Waiting for the candidate to call you back. Call them the same day.
Bidding in public. Talk to the hiring manager before you share a new number.
Using pay as the only lever. Title, scope, and review dates often matter too.
Treating a verbal yes as signed. Get the acceptance in writing.
Setting deadlines you cannot back up. Candidates notice, and it hurts trust.
Skipping the debrief. A decline tells you what to fix in the next offer.

blocks.text: The last item matters most. Ask the candidate, politely, what would have made the first offer work. Their answer is free research for your next search.
What to do after the candidate says yes or no

If they accept the counter, the work is not done. Set a check-in date, and write it in your sheet. Gallup recommends a meaningful conversation with each direct report every week. It links that habit to higher engagement, which is Gallup's own claim. Ask the hiring manager to hold a short regular talk during the first months.

If they decline, close the loop. Thank them and ask for the reason in one line. Log the answer in your tracker. The reason is often pay. It may also be career concerns, commute, timing, or a stronger offer elsewhere. Each reason points to a different fix.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It does not click buttons, edit your sheet, or send email for you. Think of it as a helper that points, guides, drafts, and listens while you work.

A good use is a moment on a live call. You cannot find the Schedule send option in Gmail. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask where it is. Lazur circles the arrow next to Send and labels it. For a full walkthrough, ask Lazur to guide you. It waits for each click before it goes on.

Dictation helps after the call. Hold fn and speak your notes. Lazur types clean text at the cursor in any app. You can also ask for a reminder by voice, such as a check-in date in Apple Reminders. You make every click and every sent email yourself.

For pay ranges, ask Lazur to research public salary pages for the role. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and comes back with a summary and a report. Open each source and check the number yourself before you use it.

blocks.title: Candidate data rules come first
blocks.text: If your company limits candidate personal data, follow those rules. Do not paste pay history, ID numbers, or health details into any AI tool unless your employer allows it. Lawyers, nurses, and accountants often face stricter client or patient data rules.
Checking pay ranges without buying anything

You need a market number before you counter. Start with your company's pay bands. Then check public job postings that list a range. Write the date and the source next to each number, so you can defend it later.

Levels.fyi sells flat-fee coaching, so its benchmarks come from a commercial source. Its benchmark data is self-reported, so treat it as a rough guide, not a verdict. Check their pricing page if you are unsure what is current.

Jobjuice is a paid reference app in the Mac App Store, listed at $14.99. It holds more than 80 color-coded cards for starting offers and raises. Its listing says it is designed for iPad and not verified for macOS, although it states a Mac requirement. Read the listing before you buy.
Edge cases for regulated and timed roles

Some roles have less room to move. Pay bands in public or unionized roles can be set by policy. In that case, a counter may be impossible without HR. Check before you promise anything. For nurses, lawyers, and accountants, follow your employer's rules on client or patient data. Do not share candidate details with any tool your policy does not clear.

Timing creates its own edge case. If a start date is close, a counter can land after you have started a replacement search. Keep one backup candidate warm, and tell them only what you can share. This is not a bluff. It keeps your pipeline moving while you talk.
A one-week plan for counteroffer calls
The plan below spreads the work across a week. Start with the sheet on day one, because every later step depends on it. Adjust the days to fit your pipeline.

faq.question: What is a candidate counteroffer?
faq.answer: A candidate counteroffer happens when a candidate asks for more after you extend an offer. It can also happen when their current employer makes a counter to keep them. Either way, the candidate is weighing your offer against another option. Plan the call before the ask arrives.

faq.question: Should I always match a counteroffer?
faq.answer: No. Match only what your company can approve, and ask what is driving the request first. SHRM notes that an offer which ignores what drives a move is unlikely to keep someone long term. A match may buy time, but it rarely fixes everything.

faq.question: How often do counteroffers work?
faq.answer: The sources disagree. A 2020 LiveCareer survey of 212 hiring managers, reported by SHRM, found 65% of employees who accepted a counteroffer stayed at least two more years. An HBR page cites CEB data that 50% leave within 12 months, but that figure is secondhand. Use both as signals, not rules.

faq.question: Can I tell a candidate what a competing offer pays?
faq.answer: Ask the candidate for the key terms, and ask what would make them stay. Do not invent or inflate a competing offer. Check your company's policy on candidate data before you write any pay figure in an email or a shared sheet.

faq.question: Is there a free way to check pay ranges on a Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Start with your company's pay bands and with public job postings that list a range. Levels.fyi sells coaching, so its benchmarks come from a commercial source. Jobjuice is a paid app, and its listing says it is not verified for macOS.

faq.question: Does Lazur click buttons or send email for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate Gmail or Google Sheets for you. It points at things, guides you one click at a time, drafts text, and dictates text at the cursor. You make the clicks and check the terms.

faq.question: What if the candidate is in a regulated role?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules on candidate and client data. Check with HR before you share pay details with any tool. Some roles follow pay bands or contracts that limit what you can offer, so ask before you promise anything.

costs.title: Replacement cost in salary terms
costs.text: Gallup estimates replacing a worker costs about 200% of salary for leaders and managers. It estimates 80% for technical professionals and 40% for frontline employees. Those are estimates, not a measure of your company. Even the low end means a lost hire costs real money, plus a slower team while you search again.

costs.title: A second search and a slower team
costs.text: Each failed counteroffer sends you back to the top of the funnel. You repeat sourcing, screening, and interviews. The hiring manager waits longer, and the team carries the gap. Preliminary BLS data put the September 2026 hires rate at 3.4%. Use that as background, not a forecast for your role.

costs.title: A counteroffer that does not stick
costs.text: A 2020 LiveCareer survey of 212 hiring managers, reported by SHRM, found that 65% of employees who accepted a counteroffer stayed at least two more years. The survey is small and employer-reported. It does not say why the others left. Treat it as a warning to fix the cause, not a forecast.

costs.title: Candidate fear of a career hit
costs.text: In a Heidrick & Struggles survey cited on an HBR page, 40% of respondents thought someone who accepted a counteroffer would see their career negatively affected. A candidate who believes that may walk away, even when the money is right. The same survey found 78% of senior executives and 80% of HR leaders said accepting a counteroffer is sometimes acceptable.

causes.title: The pay question came last
causes.text: Gallup surveyed 717 U.S. employees who voluntarily left a job in the past year. In the three months before leaving, 45% said no manager or other leader talked with them about their future. That sample is employees, not candidates. The pattern still applies. Pay talk that starts late often feels like a surprise.

causes.title: The first offer left little room
causes.text: When a first offer leaves little room, candidates push harder at the end. Pew's 2023 numbers hint at this pattern. Among workers who asked for more than their starting offer, only 28% got the pay they asked for. Pushback is often a sign the first number was short. It is not always a sign of a difficult candidate.

causes.title: Comfort with asking varies
causes.text: Pew found that 42% of women and 33% of men said they did not feel comfortable asking for higher pay. Among adults ages 18 to 29, 46% said the same. Among adults 65 and older, 19% did. A quiet candidate may still want more. Do not read silence as a yes.

causes.title: A second offer is on the table
causes.text: The candidate may hold a second offer or a counter from their current employer. That is bargaining power, and they know it. Offers often carry a deadline. Ask for the terms, the deadline, and the start date before you respond. Guessing at them wastes your best window.

causes.title: The career story is weak
causes.text: Work Institute data, cited by SHRM, found one in five employees who took a new job in 2019 cited career development concerns. SHRM also warns that an offer which ignores what drives the move is unlikely to keep the person long term. If the candidate wants a clear path, a raise alone may not hold them.

fixes.title: Ask what would make them say yes
fixes.text: Before you name a number, ask the candidate what would make them sign this week. Write the answer word for word. Some candidates want a title, a start date, or a review date more than base pay. Your reply can start with the items you can approve, then move to pay.

fixes.title: Build a one-tab offer sheet
fixes.text: Make one Google Sheets tab with these columns: Candidate ID, Offer, Ask, Gap, Max approved, Non-pay items, and Decision date. In cell D2, type =C2-B2 and copy it down. Use candidate IDs, not names, if your data rules ask for that. The sheet turns a stressful call into a short check.

fixes.title: Pre-approve a range with the hiring manager
fixes.text: Agree on a top number and a short list of non-pay items before any call. Write the decision and the date in the sheet. If the manager needs time to check, you will know how long that takes. A pre-approved range lets you answer on the same call.

fixes.title: Separate base pay from the rest
fixes.text: A counteroffer does not have to be base pay alone. Ask about a signing bonus, a review date, a title, remote days, or a start date. Confirm which items your company can offer. Offer the items that cost the least to approve first, then the rest.

fixes.title: Reply in writing the same day
fixes.text: Send a short email that restates the agreed terms. In Gmail, use the arrow next to Send > Schedule send only when the reply should land at a set time. Otherwise, send it when you finish. Ask for a written reply by a set date.

fixes.title: Hold a regular talk after the hire
fixes.text: Ask the hiring manager to hold a short weekly conversation during the first months. Gallup recommends meaningful weekly talks with each direct report, and links that habit to higher engagement. That link is Gallup's own correlational claim, so treat it as a reason to try, not proof.

fixes.title: Run a short debrief on every decline
fixes.text: When a candidate declines, ask one question: what would have changed your answer? Log the reason as pay, title, scope, timing, or other offer. After a few weeks, the pattern shows what to change in your next offer.

fixes.title: Check benchmarks against a method
fixes.text: Start with your company's pay bands. Then check public job postings that list a range. Write the date and source next to every number. Levels.fyi sells coaching and self-reports its benchmark data, so treat its figures as a rough guide.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Build the offer sheet
plan.text: Open Google Sheets and create one tab for every open offer. Add columns for offer, ask, gap, max approved, non-pay items, and decision date. Use candidate IDs if your data rules require them.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Agree the range
plan.text: Book a short meeting with the hiring manager. Agree the top number, the non-pay items, and who signs off. Write the decision and its date in the sheet.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Script the first call
plan.text: Write three questions: what would make you say yes, what is driving the change, and when is the deadline. Keep the script open in a doc. Keep it short enough to scan mid-call.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Make the call and log it
plan.text: Call the candidate the same day they raise the ask. Restate the ask, then say what you can approve. Log the answer in the sheet before you move on to the next task.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Send the terms in writing
plan.text: Email the agreed terms the same day. Use Schedule send only if the timing matters. Ask for a written reply by a set date, and put that date in the sheet.

plan.label: Week 2
plan.title: Check in on the new hire
plan.text: Set a reminder for the check-in date. Ask the hiring manager for a short regular talk during the first months. Note any new risk in the sheet so it does not get lost.
